Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

TEHRAN, Iran (CNN) -- A well-known Iranian filmmaker has written an open letter calling for the release of journalist Roxana Saberi. In a letter, Iranian filmmaker Bahman Ghobadi blames himself for urging Roxana Saberi to stay in Iran. Bahman Ghobadi said he kept quiet about the arrest and conviction of the Iranian-American journalist at the request of her family. After Saberi was convicted last weekend and sentenced to an eight-year prison sentence, he said he felt he had to do something. He told CNN that Saberi, whom he described as his fiancee, is caught in a "game of politics." In his letter, which has been posted by the International Campaign for Human Rights in Iran, Ghobadi blames himself for urging Saberi to stay in Iran despite her desire to leave. Also, he writes, "My letter is a desperate call to all statesmen ... and to all those who can do something to help." "From the other side of the ocean, the Americans have protested against her imprisonment, because she is an American citizen," he writes. "But I say no, she is Iranian, and she loves Iran. I beg you, let her go! I beg you not to throw her in the midst of your political games! She is too weak and too pure to take part in your games. Let me be present at her trial, sit next to her wise father and gentle mother, and testify she is without guilt or reproach." The 40-year-old filmmaker said that Saberi was planning to leave the country, but he kept her from leaving until his latest film -- which will be shown at this year's Cannes film festival -- was completed. Ghobadi won the 2000 Golden Camera award at the Cannes festival for his feature film, "A Time for Drunken Horses." Saberi, 31, was sentenced Saturday to eight years in prison after a one-day trial that was closed to the public. The decision prompted sharp denunciations from President Barack Obama, as well as other U.S. and international officials. Iranian officials initially said Saberi was held for buying a bottle of wine. The Foreign Ministry later said she was detained for reporting without proper accreditation. On April 9, word emerged that Saberi had been charged with espionage. Saberi's lawyer has said he will appeal the verdict. Judiciary Chief Ayatollah Hashemi Shahroudi has ordered the head of Tehran's Justice Department to make sure the appeals process is quick and fair. Ghobadi wrote that he is "optimistic about her release, and I firmly hope the verdict will be canceled in the next stage of the trial." "My Iranian girl with Japanese eyes and an American ID, is in jail. Shame on me! Shame on us!" CNN's Igor Krotov and Shirzad Bozorghmehr contributed to this report.

# Renowned Iranian Filmmaker Pens Impassioned Plea for Journalist's Release

**TEHRAN, Iran (CNN)** — A prominent Iranian filmmaker has issued an open letter appealing for the release of journalist Roxana Saberi, in which he holds himself partly responsible for encouraging her to remain in the country. Bahman Ghobadi revealed that he had refrained from publicly addressing Saberi's arrest and conviction at the request of her family. However, following her conviction last weekend and subsequent eight-year prison sentence, he felt compelled to speak out. In an interview with CNN, Ghobadi—who described Saberi as his fiancée—characterized her situation as being ensnared in a "game of politics."

In the letter, published by the International Campaign for Human Rights in Iran, Ghobadi expresses profound remorse for having persuaded Saberi to stay in Iran despite her wishes to depart. "My letter is a desperate call to all statesmen," he writes, "and to all those who can do something to help."

He continues: "From the other side of the ocean, the Americans have protested against her imprisonment, because she is an American citizen. But I say no—she is Iranian, and she loves Iran. I beg you, let her go! I beg you not to throw her into the midst of your political games! She is too weak and too pure to take part in your games. Let me be present at her trial, sit next to her wise father and gentle mother, and testify that she is without guilt or reproach."

The 40-year-old director explained that Saberi had intended to leave Iran, but he had persuaded her to delay her departure until the completion of his latest film, which is set to premiere at this year's Cannes Film Festival. Ghobadi previously received the Caméra d'Or at Cannes in 2000 for his feature "A Time for Drunken Horses."

Saberi, 31, was sentenced Saturday to eight years' imprisonment following a one-day trial held behind closed doors—a decision that drew sharp condemnation from President Barack Obama and numerous other American and international officials. Iranian authorities initially claimed Saberi had been detained for purchasing a bottle of wine; the Foreign Ministry later revised this account, stating she had been held for reporting without valid press credentials. On April 9, it emerged that she had, in fact, been charged with espionage.

Saberi's attorney has indicated his intent to appeal the verdict. Judiciary Chief Ayatollah Hashemi Shahroudi has since directed the head of Tehran's Justice Department to ensure the appeals process proceeds both swiftly and fairly.

In closing, Ghobadi expressed cautious optimism: "I am optimistic about her release, and I firmly hope the verdict will be overturned in the next stage of the trial. My Iranian girl with Japanese eyes and an American ID is in jail. Shame on me! Shame on us!"

# An Open Letter from the Heart: Bahman Ghobadi's Plea for Roxana Saberi

In a deeply personal and emotionally charged appeal, acclaimed Iranian filmmaker Bahman Ghobadi has broken his silence to advocate for the release of journalist Roxana Saberi, revealing in an open letter that the imprisoned reporter is, in fact, his fiancée. The disclosure adds a profoundly personal dimension to what has already become an internationally watched legal and diplomatic controversy.

## A Confession of Guilt

Perhaps the most striking aspect of Ghobadi's letter is his willingness to shoulder personal blame for Saberi's predicament. He candidly admitted that he had repeatedly urged her to remain in Iran, even though she had expressed a clear desire to leave the country. According to Ghobadi, his own professional commitments played a direct role in delaying her departure—he asked her to stay until the completion of his latest film project. This admission reveals a filmmaker wrestling not only with the anguish of seeing a loved one imprisoned, but also with the weight of feeling personally responsible for the circumstances that led to her continued presence in Iran during a period of escalating risk.

## Breaking a Self-Imposed Silence

Ghobadi explained that his public reticence throughout Saberi's arrest and subsequent conviction was not born of indifference, but of respect—he had honored a request from her family to remain quiet, presumably to avoid complicating an already sensitive legal situation. However, the imposition of an eight-year prison sentence proved to be a breaking point. The severity of the punishment, he indicated, made continued silence untenable, compelling him to speak publicly and advocate on her behalf despite the risks that such a high-profile intervention might carry.

## A Pawn in Political Games

At the core of Ghobadi's argument is a forceful assertion that Saberi has become entangled in matters far beyond her control—what he characterized as a "game of politics." He implored Iranian authorities not to treat her as a political bargaining chip, emphatically maintaining her innocence and framing her prosecution as fundamentally disconnected from any genuine wrongdoing on her part. His appeal frames Saberi not as a criminal defendant, but as a victim of geopolitical tensions between Iran and the West, caught in circumstances that have little to do with journalism or the law and much to do with broader diplomatic friction.

## International Backlash

Saberi's case has not remained confined to personal or domestic Iranian concerns; it has escalated into a matter of significant international attention. Her conviction, delivered after a trial that lasted only a single day and was conducted behind closed doors, has been met with sharp criticism from around the world. President Barack Obama personally condemned the verdict, adding the weight of the American presidency to a growing chorus of international disapproval. Numerous other U.S. officials and figures within the broader international community have echoed these concerns, questioning the fairness and transparency of judicial proceedings that produced such a severe sentence in such an expedited and opaque manner.

Together, these elements—a filmmaker's personal guilt, a family's plea for silence now broken, and a wave of international condemnation—have transformed Roxana Saberi's case into a flashpoint that intertwines personal tragedy with pressing questions about justice, press freedom, and the political dynamics shaping Iran's relationship with the wider world.

CNN, as one of the world's most prominent international news networks, has maintained a complex relationship with reporting from Iran. Access to Tehran for Western journalists has historically been restricted and carefully managed by Iranian authorities, making any on-the-ground reporting from the network particularly significant. When CNN correspondents have been granted access to Tehran, their reports often provide rare glimpses into daily life, political developments, and the perspectives of ordinary Iranians that might otherwise remain unseen by international audiences.

The coverage of Iran by outlets like CNN typically spans several critical areas: the ongoing nuclear negotiations and their implications for regional stability, Iran's relationship with Western powers, domestic protests and human rights concerns, and the country's economic challenges under international sanctions. Each of these topics requires careful, nuanced reporting given the sensitivities involved.

Tehran itself tells a story of contrasts—a city where ancient Persian culture meets modern urban development, where political conservatism coexists with a young, increasingly connected population eager for global engagement. When CNN's cameras capture scenes from Tehran's streets, markets, or press conferences, they offer viewers a window into a nation that remains, for many in the West, shrouded in both mystery and geopolitical significance.

The relationship between international media and Iranian authorities remains delicate. Access is often granted selectively, and the Iranian government maintains strict oversight of what foreign journalists can document. This dynamic shapes not only what stories emerge from Tehran but how they're framed for international audiences, making media literacy and cross-referencing multiple sources essential for anyone seeking to understand the full picture of contemporary Iran.

As geopolitical tensions and diplomatic developments continue to evolve, Tehran will likely remain a focal point for international news coverage, with networks like CNN continuing to navigate the challenges of reporting accurately and responsibly from one of the world's most closely scrutinized capitals.

Ghobadi, known internationally for films such as "Turtles Can Fly" and "A Time for Drunken Horses," worked closely with Saberi in Iran, where she had lived and worked as a freelance journalist for several years, reporting for outlets including National Public Radio and the BBC. In his letter, Ghobadi described Saberi as a woman of integrity who loved Iran and its people, and he expressed deep personal anguish over her imprisonment.

"I have known Roxana for years, and I can say with certainty that she is not a spy, nor an enemy of my country," Ghobadi wrote. "She came to Iran to tell its stories to the world — stories of its culture, its people, its struggles and its beauty. To imprison her is to imprison the truth."

Saberi, 31, was initially detained on allegations of buying alcohol, a charge her father has called a pretext. Iranian authorities later accused her of working without valid press credentials after her original license expired, and most recently leveled the far more serious charge of espionage, an accusation that could carry a lengthy prison sentence.

The journalist, who holds dual American and Iranian citizenship, was born in the United States to an Iranian father and a Japanese mother. She had been living in Iran since 2003, and was reportedly working on a book about the country at the time of her arrest.

Ghobadi's letter, which has circulated widely among journalists, human rights advocates and members of the Iranian artistic community, adds a prominent cultural voice to the growing chorus demanding Saberi's release. The filmmaker, whose work often explores themes of injustice and the plight of marginalized communities in the Middle East, has not been shy about criticizing the Iranian government in the past, though he continues to live and work in the country.

"As someone who has dedicated his life and his art to telling the truth of this land, I understand the risks journalists take," Ghobadi wrote. "Roxana took those risks not out of malice, but out of love and curiosity for a country that is not always her own, yet is also entirely her own."

The case has drawn condemnation from press freedom organizations, including the Committee to Protect Journalists and Reporters Without Borders, both of which have called the charges against Saberi politically motivated. The U.S. State Department has also repeatedly urged Iranian authorities to release her, calling the allegations "baseless."

Saberi's parents, Reza and Akiko Saberi, traveled to Tehran shortly after her detention and have been granted limited visitation rights. In statements to reporters, they have expressed concern over their daughter's health and the conditions of her confinement, while maintaining hope that international pressure will lead to her release.

Iran's government has not publicly responded to Ghobadi's letter, though state media has continued to report on the espionage allegations without providing detailed evidence.

Saberi's trial, held partially behind closed doors, has been criticized by human rights groups for lacking transparency. A verdict has not yet been announced, and it remains unclear when one might be issued.

Ghobadi closed his letter with a direct appeal to Iranian officials: "Let her go. Let her return to her family, to her work, to her life. Iran does not need another prisoner of conscience — it needs to show the world it still values justice and mercy."
